newsitem.title: FRANCE: Sword of justice hangs over French poll campaign.
newsitem.headline: Sword of justice hangs over French poll campaign.

text.p: The shadow of magistrates probing political corruption looms over France's parliamentary election campaign -- a threat to both right and left and a potential boost to the extreme right.
Charges of illicit funding of most major parties through rake-offs on public contracts have plagued France for years.
The scandals hit the Socialists first, playing a major role in their 1993 election rout.

The spotlight has since shifted to the ruling centre-right coalition, and Socialist leader Lionel Jospin was quick to suggest that President Jacques Chirac had called a snap election partly because he feared new scandals could be exposed.

"We are told the government fears being caught by scandals that effectively threaten several cabinet members and, through the Paris city hall, very important figures of the majority," the opposition chief said.
Media reports denied by both men said Finance Minister Jean Arthuis and Social Affairs Minister Jacques Barrot could soon be placed under investigation over the finances of the centrist CDS party.
An early election would give Chirac the option of simply not reappointing them to government if the coalition wins.

Investigating magistrate Eric Halphen is doggedly probing Chirac's RPR party on suspicion that it systematically extorted kickbacks on public works contracts in the Paris region while the president was mayor from 1977 to 1995.
Louise-Yvonne Casetta, the RPR's former personnel chief and unofficial treasurer, and dozens of businessmen have been placed under investigation on suspicion of misusing corporate funds.

Halphen raided RPR headquarters this month in search of evidence. His probe has extended to Chirac's successor as mayor, Jean Tiberi, and Tiberi's wife Xaviere, who are under judicial investigation on suspicion of unduly receiving public funds.

In a measure of its embarrassment over the Tiberi case, the government chartered a helicopter to try to track down a state prosecutor trekking in Nepal last year in a bungled bid to head off the probe launched by his independent-minded deputy.
The head of criminal police, Olivier Foll, barred his men from helping Halphen search the mayor's home.
New developments in the probes during the election campaign could be damaging for the coalition, some of whose leading members were convicted in separate sleaze probes recently.

The former mayors of Grenoble and Lyon, Alain Carignon and Michel Mouillot, are behind bars for sleaze and ex-Lyon mayor Michel Noir was forced to quit politics after receiving an 18-month suspended sentence.
Housing scandals in which Prime Minister Alain Juppe and his family, as well as Tiberi's children, were found to be living in low-rent luxury city-owned homes have also been damaging.
But the Socialists may be wary of using sleaze charges as election ammunition as the spotlight shifts back to them at the height of the campaign, between the two rounds of voting.

A Lyon court will rule on May 29 on an illicit fundraising scheme involving ex-Socialist party leader and treasurer Henri Emmanuelli. He has already been given a one-year suspended sentence in a related case and faces an 18-month suspended term with a ban on standing for public office.
The Socialists are also embarrassed by a scandal over illegal wiretapping of private citizens ordered by the late president Francois Mitterrand in the 1980s.

A special court is still investigating whether Socialist ex-premier Laurent Fabius and two of his ex-ministers will face charges of poisoning over the 1980s distribution of AIDS-tainted blood products which killed hundreds of haemophiliacs.
The Communists may also be tamed by a probe underway into leader Robert Hue and his predecessor Georges Marchais for party receipts from local water contracts in some 70 towns.
The far-right National Front, the only major party that has so far escaped charges of illicit financing, has long used sleaze charges to attack the political establishment.

Its leader Jean-Marie Le Pen indicated corruption would be a major argument in his campaign, saying in reply to Chirac's announcement of the snap election: "He knows that the judicial probes into the RPR could soon get to him."
